subject: Dolichopteryx longipes refractive-reflective eye
structure_mechanism: split tubular eye combining an upward lens-based optical path with a ventrally directed diverticulum focused by a curved multilayer mirror derived from retinal tapetum
claim: Dolichopteryx longipes forms a focused image with a mirror inside a vertebrate eye: progressively changing reflective-plate angles redirect ventral light onto a lateral retina, while the main tubular portion retains conventional refractive optics. This is a genuine refractive/reflective hybrid rather than an animal simply possessing a reflective tapetum.

quantitative.depth_context_m: mesopelagic; specimen underlying the optical study was collected at ~800 m

function: simultaneous sampling of downwelling light above and faint/bio-luminescent sources below in a low-light pelagic environment
limitations: The optical study demonstrates anatomy and modeled image formation; behavioral acuity and ecological detection thresholds were not directly measured. Popular claims that it has four independent eyes are anatomically misleading: it has paired eyes with distinct optical fields.
contradictions: Popular 'four-eyed fish' descriptions overstate the anatomy; the important novelty is two optical systems within each paired eye.

sources.title: A novel vertebrate eye using both refractive and reflective optics
sources.authors: Hans-Joachim Wagner; Ron H Douglas; Tamara M Frank; Nicholas W Roberts; Julian C Partridge

subject: high-resolution object vision in pelagic alciopid polychaetes
species_group: Alciopini (pelagic polychaete annelids; three night-active Mediterranean species)
structure_mechanism: large paired camera-type eyes with primary retina; optical, morphological and electrophysiological specialization for spatial and temporal performance
claim: Night-active pelagic alciopid worms provide evidence for high spatial acuity together with high temporal resolution in annelids, expanding high-resolution object vision beyond the animal lineages in which it was traditionally considered conclusively established. The result is especially notable because these are annelids, not arthropods or cephalopods.
function: active object vision in the pelagic nocturnal environment; the exact natural targets and behavioral tasks remain under investigation
limitations: The 2024 study supports the optical/electrophysiological capacity for high-resolution object vision, but does not establish the complete behavioral repertoire or prove equivalence to vertebrate, arthropod or cephalopod object vision. Claims that this alone establishes a universally accepted 'fourth phylum with high-resolution vision' should therefore be phrased cautiously.
contradictions: Capacity inferred from optics, morphology and electrophysiology should not be inflated into proof of all class-IV visually guided behaviors.

sources.title: High-resolution vision in pelagic polychaetes
sources.authors: Michael J Bok; Armando Macali; Anders Garm

subject: optical scanning in Copilia lateral eyes
structure_mechanism: large anterior lens with very few receptors that move through the focused image plane, implementing mechanical optical scanning
claim: Female Copilia quadrata does not obtain spatial sampling from a dense stationary receptor mosaic: a tiny receptor structure scans the image formed by the anterior lens. Optical measurements in intact animals placed the focused image near the distal receptor ends and provided evidence that receptor movement participates in vision.

quantitative.receptor_array: very few receptors; the primary paper emphasizes sparse receptor sampling rather than a conventional dense retina

function: narrow-field target acquisition in a small pelagic copepod, historically associated with detection of biologically relevant objects such as mates or prey
limitations: The core behavioral/optical experiment is old (1972), and the exact neural reconstruction of a scanned scene is not established by that study. Calling it a biological television camera is an analogy, not a demonstrated equivalence in encoding architecture.
contradictions: Mechanical scanning does not imply a high-pixel-count retina; its novelty is precisely that spatial information is sampled sequentially with very few receptors.

sources.title: Optical Scanning in the Lateral Eyes of the Copepod Copilia
